Put the script and a `data/` folder holding `pine_data.csv` in your project, then run the script from top to bottom.

## What these tests do

A t-test compares a **mean** to something: a fixed number (one-sample), another group's mean (two-sample), or the same unit measured twice (paired). Each one asks whether a difference is bigger than chance would produce.

| Test | Question | R call |
|----|----|----|
| One-sample | Is the mean different from a number? | `t.test(x, mu = 15)` |
| Two-sample | Do two group means differ? | `t.test(y ~ group, var.equal = TRUE)` |
| Welch | Same, but variances may differ | `t.test(y ~ group, var.equal = FALSE)` |
| Paired | Is the mean *difference* within pairs zero? | `t.test(a, b, paired = TRUE)` |

**Data:** pine needle lengths (mm) from the sunny and shady sides of trees, 8 needles per side per tree, one tree per team.

## Step 1: Load packages and data

```{r}
#| label: step-1-load
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(car)   # leveneTest(), qqPlot()

pine_df <- read_csv("data/pine_data.csv")

pine_df
```

## Step 2: Average away the pseudoreplicates

The 8 needles from one side of one tree are not independent. Average them so each tree-side is **one** data point.

```{r}
#| label: step-2-average
#| message: false
p_df <- pine_df %>%
  group_by(team, side) %>%
  summarise(needle_length_mm = mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

p_df
```

## Step 3: Summary statistics

```{r}
#| label: step-3-summary
stats_df <- p_df %>%
  group_by(side) %>%
  summarize(
    n    = sum(!is.na(needle_length_mm)),
    mean = mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd   = sd(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    se   = sd / sqrt(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
stats_df
```

## Step 4: Plot the data

Always plot before testing. The boxplot shows spread and outliers; the slope plot shows the pairing (one line per tree).

```{r}
#| label: step-4-plots
#| fig-width: 3.2
#| fig-height: 2.8
box_plot <- p_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(side, needle_length_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw()
box_plot

slope_plot <- p_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(side, needle_length_mm, group = team)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw()
slope_plot
```

## Step 5: One-sample t-test

**Question:** is the mean shady-side needle length different from 15 mm?

$H_0: \mu = 15$ vs. $H_A: \mu \neq 15$

```{r}
#| label: step-5a-check-normal
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 2.8
shady_df <- p_df %>% filter(side == "shady")
sunny_df <- p_df %>% filter(side == "sunny")

# assumption: the shady values are roughly normal
qqPlot(shady_df$needle_length_mm)
shapiro.test(shady_df$needle_length_mm)
```

```{r}
#| label: step-5b-one-sample
one_sample_model <- t.test(shady_df$needle_length_mm, mu = 15)
one_sample_model
```

For a one-tailed test, add `alternative = "less"` or `"greater"`:

```{r}
#| label: step-5c-one-tailed
t.test(shady_df$needle_length_mm, mu = 15, alternative = "less")
```

## Step 6: Two-sample t-test

**Question:** does mean needle length differ between sides?

$H_0: \mu_{shady} = \mu_{sunny}$ vs. $H_A: \mu_{shady} \neq \mu_{sunny}$

**Check the assumptions** — normality within each group and equal variances:

```{r}
#| label: step-6a-assumptions
#| warning: false
p_df %>%
  group_by(side) %>%
  summarize(shapiro_p = shapiro.test(needle_length_mm)$p.value,
            .groups = "drop")

leveneTest(needle_length_mm ~ factor(side), data = p_df)
```

Both p > 0.05 means no evidence against normality or equal variances. With only 4 points per side, these tests have very little power, so **look at the plots too**.

```{r}
#| label: step-6b-two-sample
two_sample_model <- t.test(needle_length_mm ~ side,
                           data = p_df, var.equal = TRUE)
two_sample_model
```

## Step 7: Welch's t-test

Welch's version does not assume equal variances. It is R's default (`var.equal = FALSE`) and is a safe choice whenever Levene's test or the boxplot suggests unequal spread.

```{r}
#| label: step-7-welch
welch_model <- t.test(needle_length_mm ~ side,
                      data = p_df, var.equal = FALSE)
welch_model
```

Note the fractional df. That is the Welch correction.

## Step 8: Paired t-test

Both sides were measured on the **same tree**, so the right test pairs them. First make one column per side:

```{r}
#| label: step-8a-wide
p_wide_df <- p_df %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = side,
              values_from = needle_length_mm)
p_wide_df
```

```{r}
#| label: step-8b-paired
paired_model <- t.test(p_wide_df$shady,
                       p_wide_df$sunny,
                       paired = TRUE)
paired_model
```

A paired t-test is the same as a one-sample t-test on the differences:

```{r}
#| label: step-8c-differences
diff_df <- p_wide_df %>%
  mutate(difference = sunny - shady)

t.test(diff_df$difference, mu = 0)
```

## Step 9: Reading the output

- **t**: the difference divided by its standard error. Bigger \|t\| means stronger evidence.
- **df**: n − 1 (one-sample, paired), n₁ + n₂ − 2 (two-sample), or a fractional value (Welch).
- **p-value**: the chance of a t this extreme if $H_0$ were true. Below 0.05, reject $H_0$.
- **95% CI**: the plausible range for the mean (or difference). If it excludes the null value, p < 0.05.

Pairing removes tree-to-tree variation, so the paired test has a much smaller standard error than the two-sample test on the same numbers. Compare the two p-values.

## Step 10: Write it up

> Sunny-side needles were on average `r round(-paired_model$estimate, 2)` mm longer than shady-side needles, but the difference was not significant (paired t-test: t(`r paired_model$parameter`) = `r round(paired_model$statistic, 2)`, p = `r signif(paired_model$p.value, 2)`, n = 4 trees; 95% CI for shady − sunny: `r round(paired_model$conf.int[1], 2)` to `r round(paired_model$conf.int[2], 2)` mm).

Give the test, t, df, p, n, and the size of the effect with its CI. Report means ± SE from Step 3 in a table or figure. With only 4 trees, a non-significant result says little; the CI shows how wide the uncertainty is.
